one_liner: Two-file C89 JSON DOM with dot-path access; parsed 1.85x faster than JsonCpp 1.0.0 in a 2016 run, mostly on number-heavy canada.json.
what_it_does: Parson parses a NUL-terminated string or file into a tree of JSON_Value nodes (json_parse_string, json_parse_file, plus _with_comments variants that strip /* */ and // first) and serializes it back compactly or pretty-printed to a malloc'd string, a caller buffer or a file. Values are read and written through typed getters and setters, including dot-notation paths such as json_object_dotget_string(obj, "commit.author.name") that also create intermediate objects on set. It adds deep copy, equality and a simple shape check (json_validate, not JSON Schema). It is a C API, not a drop-in for JsonCpp's C++ Json::Value.
how_it_is_fast: It is not built for speed: the parser walks the input with a char pointer, calls strtod directly on the buffer for numbers, and mallocs every node separately (each string twice: a worst-case buffer, then a trimmed copy). Its 2016 parse lead over JsonCpp 1.0.0 and json-c 0.12.1 comes almost entirely from canada.json, the number-heavy file (64.6 vs 142.5 and 105.8 ms). Serialization is slow by design: json_serialize_to_string runs a full size-computing pass, then json_serialize_to_buffer runs that pass again before the writing pass, so every number goes through sprintf("%1.17g") three times; that matches its 110.9 ms stringify total against json-c's 30.8 ms in the same run.
when_to_use: C or C++ projects that want two files to vendor (parson.c, parson.h), C89 compatibility and an MIT licence for reading configs or API responses in the KB to low-MB range.
Code that addresses nested fields by path: json_object_dotget_* and json_object_dotset_* replace chains of lookups and auto-create intermediate objects.

Memory-constrained parsing where JsonCpp or json-c are the alternative: the 2016 run used 9.1 MB for the three files against 24.6 MB (JsonCpp) and 49.9 MB (json-c), and json_set_allocation_functions plugs in a custom allocator.
Config files with comments, through json_parse_string_with_comments / json_parse_file_with_comments.
when_not_to_use: Parse throughput: in the 2016 CSV cJSON parsed the same three files in 24.7 ms, udp/json-parser in 47.3 ms and RapidJSON in 7.9 ms against Parson's 89.5 ms, and Parson lost to JsonCpp and Qt on citm_catalog.json and to json-c and Qt on twitter.json.

Serialization-heavy work: stringify was slower than JsonCpp, nlohmann/json 2.0.3 and json-c (3.6x) in 2016, and zzzJSON's later table (i7-6700, g++ 7.3 -O3, versions not stated) has Parson at 857 ms stringify across its corpora against 431 ms for JsonCpp and 217 ms for nlohmann.

Strict validation of untrusted JSON: since 1.4.0 (2022-03-06) it accepts trailing commas in arrays and objects, json_parse_string parses only the first value and ignores trailing text, and object keys are hashed with an unseeded djb2 hash and linear probing, so crafted colliding keys can make large-object parsing quadratic.
Documents with duplicate keys: json_object_add refuses a key already present, so the whole parse returns NULL instead of keeping the first or last value.

Non-NUL-terminated buffers or programs that change LC_NUMERIC: there is no length-bounded parse call, and strtod/sprintf follow the C locale, so a comma-decimal locale breaks number parsing and output.

integration.form: source-drop (parson.c + parson.h); CMake and meson files also build a static or shared library
integration.min_toolchain: C89 compiler (tests build with -std=c89 -pedantic-errors and as C++ with g++); CMake 3.5+ or meson 0.46+ if used
integration.platforms: any; a 2023 fix (1.5.3) covers macOS sprintf deprecation and CI runs on GitHub Actions
integration.thread_safety: Separate values can be parsed and serialized concurrently, but the allocator hooks, slash escaping, float format and number-serializer settings are process globals; the header says json_set_escape_slashes is not thread safe and json_set_allocation_functions must be called once before any other call.

gotchas: The measured revision is not today's code: nativejson-benchmark pins c22be79 (2016), whose parson.c stored objects as arrays with a linear duplicate-key scan and hard limits of 960 keys per object (OBJECT_MAX_CAPACITY), 122,880 elements per array and 19 levels of nesting; objects became hash maps in 1.2.0 (2021-08-05), MAX_NESTING is now 2048, and serialization changed in 2021 and 1.5.0 (2022). Current speed relative to JsonCpp is unmeasured.

Harness flaws (not in the catalogued parse claim): the suite's Parson Prettify calls json_serialize_to_string, the compact serializer, so that row is void; and its Statistics walk looks every member up by name with json_object_get_value(o, name) instead of json_object_get_value_at(o, i), a linear scan per member against the 2016 object arrays, so Parson's statistics rows (0.997 ms on twitter.json against 0.090 for PicoJSON) measure the harness, not the DOM.

Slashes are escaped as \/ on output unless json_set_escape_slashes(0) is called, numbers print with %1.17g (1.2345 becomes 1.2344999999999999), and 13 of 27 round-trip and 3 of 34 parse-validation tests failed in the 2016 run (trailing text after the first value was accepted).

Recent memory-safety fixes: an out-of-bounds read in is_valid_utf8 on truncated multi-byte sequences was fixed on 2026-09-15 (1.5.4), after earlier reports of a stack buffer overflow in parson_sprintf (#221) and an out-of-bounds read on unterminated strings (#222); use 1.5.4 or later for untrusted input.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Parson over cJSON, Jansson or json-c when dot-path access, a two-file C89 drop-in and low parse memory matter more than speed; pick cJSON (3.6x faster parse in the same 2016 run) or udp/json-parser for parse speed, json-c for serialization (3.6x faster stringify), and yyjson when throughput is the goal.
verified_claims_summary: In nativejson-benchmark's committed 2016 sample (Apple clang 7.0, optimize Full with -march=native, Core i7-4980HQ, macOS), the 2016 Parson revision c22be79 parsed canada, citm_catalog and twitter in 89.5 ms total against JsonCpp 1.0.0's 165.5 ms (1.85x), json-c 0.12.1's 134.6 ms (1.50x) and Qt 5.6's 125.0 ms (1.40x), a lead that comes from canada.json; it was slower than nlohmann/json 2.0.3, cJSON and RapidJSON, and its stringify was slower than every library but Qt. The project makes no speed claim.
status_note: Active (1.5.4 on 2026-09-15 with a memory-safety fix), MIT, two files and easy to vendor; the speed entry rests on a 2016 run of a pre-hash-map revision against 2016 baselines, so treat it as a lightweight-API pick rather than a speed pick.
